Type the letter of your choice.

A bearing is always measured clockwise from which direction?
A) East
B) South
C) North
D) West
c

Exactly — every bearing starts at north and sweeps clockwise, so 0° and 360° both point north. That's why a sailor can name any direction with a single number between 000° and 360°.

Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between compass points and bearings?
A) Compass points and bearings are the same thing expressed differently.
B) Bearings are compass points that have been converted to degrees.
C) Compass points are verbal directions, while bearings are precise numerical measurements from north.
D) Compass points are used only on nautical maps, while bearings are used on land maps.
c

Exactly — words like "northeast" give a general direction, while a bearing pins it down in degrees measured clockwise from north. Now use that precision on a real reading:

**A seafarer records a bearing of 163° to a navigation marker. Which of the following best describes the general direction of the marker?**
A) Slightly south of east (E-SE)
B) Slightly south of due south (S-SE)
C) Slightly east of due south (S-SE)
D) Slightly east of due east (E-SE)
i think b

Not quite — check which side of due south 163° falls on. Due south is 180°, and bearings grow clockwise from North, so a bearing *less* than 180° hasn't reached south yet. Which side of due south does that put the marker on — east or west?
oh wait, east. so it's slightly east of due south right? that's c

Yes — that's the right way to read it: a bearing under 180° hasn't swung past due south yet, so it sits on the eastern side of it. Note the wording trap too: one option says "south of due south," which isn't a real position on the compass. Enter your choice now and I'll check it.
c

Got it — that's right. Here's the next one:

What is the bearing equivalent of the compass point Southwest (SW)?
A) 135°
B) 225°
C) 315°
D) 45°

Correct — nice work. Try this one:

A bearing of 315° corresponds to which compass point?
A) Northeast (NE)
B) Northwest (NW)
C) Southeast (SE)
D) Southwest (SW)
a

Not quite — bearings run clockwise from north (000°), so 090° is east, 180° is south, and 270° is west. Since 315° sits past 270°, it falls between west and north, not between north and east — which compass point lies in that quarter?
oh right, northwest. so b

Pick the letter that matches one complete turn.

What is the sum of all angles around a point?
A) 270°
B) 180°
C) 450°
D) 360°
d

Exactly — one full spin brings you right back to where you started, and that's 360°. So if you know all but one angle around a point, you can always find the missing one by subtracting from 360.

Four angles around a point measure 70°, 50°, 90°, and x°. What is x?
A) 150°
B) -30°
C) 30°
D) 120°
ok so i add up the ones i know. 70 plus 50 is 120, then 120 plus 90 is 210. then 360 minus 210 is 150. so a

Exactly — you summed the knowns and took them from the full turn of 360°. Same rule, but now with only two angles given.

Three angles around a point are 80°, 50°, and x°. What is x?
A) 130°
B) 40°
C) 230°
D) 50°
80 plus 50 is 130. then 360 minus 130 is 230. so c

Five angles around a point are 50°, 80°, 60°, 50°, and m°. Find m.
A) 240°
B) 170°
C) 50°
D) 120°
ok so 50 plus 80 is 130, then 130 plus 60 is 190, then 190 plus 50 is 240. then 360 minus 240 is 120. so d

Spot on — you added all four known angles first, then subtracted from 360°, which works no matter how many angles surround the point. Keep that same two-step routine going here:

A surveyor in Seychelles marks four angles around a survey point: 75°, 85°, 95°, and x°. Calculate x.
A) 155° B) -75° C) 285° D) 105°

A) 155°
B) -75°
C) 285°
D) 105°
75 plus 85 is 160, then 160 plus 95 is 255. then 360 minus 255 is 105. so d

Exactly — clean running total, then subtract from 360°. The same rule holds no matter how many angles meet at the point, so let's stretch it to five.

Five angles around a point measure 50°, 55°, 70°, 65°, and y. Calculate y.
ok so 50 plus 55 is 105, then 105 plus 70 is 175, then 175 plus 65 is 240. then 360 minus 240 is 120. so y is 120

Spot on — clean running total, then subtract from 360°. Now the special case: when angles sit **on a straight line** rather than all the way around a point, they only go half-way round, so they add to 180° — like looking from one end of the horizon to the other.

On a straight line, angle A is 120°. What is the supplementary angle?
oh so on a line it's 180 not 360. so 180 minus 120 is 60. the other angle is 60
Three angles sit on a straight line. Two angles measure 45° and 65°. What is the third angle?
ok so 45 plus 65 is 110. then 180 minus 110 is 70. so the third angle is 70

Spot on — clean subtraction from 180° for a straight line. Now switch to the full turn: angles around a point close up all the way to 360°.

Four angles around a point are 80°, 60°, 70°, and x°. Find x.
80 plus 60 is 140, then 140 plus 70 is 210. then 360 minus 210 is 150. so x is 150

Spot on — adding the knowns first and subtracting from 360° is exactly the method.

At a roundabout in Victoria, Seychelles, roads branch off in four directions creating four angles around the central point. The angles measure 85°, 92°, 88°, and x. Find x to determine all angles at the roundabout.
85 plus 92 is 177, then 177 plus 88 is 265. then 360 minus 265 is 95. so x is 95

Here's your warm-up: **What does a map scale of 1:25,000 indicate?**

A) 1 centimetre on the map represents 25,000 centimetres on the ground

C) 25,000 maps are needed to cover the ground area
D) The map covers an area of 25,000 square kilometres
a, because 1 centimetre equals 25,000 centimetres

Exactly — and 25,000 cm works out to 250 m, so the ratio unit stays the same on both sides. Now let's push that idea to comparing two maps of the same place.

If a large-scale map (1:10,000) and a small-scale map (1:500,000) both show the same geographic area, which statement is correct?
A) The small-scale map shows more detail and requires less area on the paper
B) The large-scale map shows more detail and covers a smaller paper area for the same ground region
C) Both maps show the same level of detail and cover the same paper area
D) The small-scale map shows more detail because the scale number is larger
d, because the scale number is bigger so it shows more detail

Careful — the ratio 1:500,000 means 1 cm stands for 500,000 cm on the ground, so a bigger second number squeezes *more* ground onto the same paper. Think about what happens to detail when you squeeze a huge area onto one sheet, then look again at the four statements.
ohh wait, so b then, because the large scale map shows more detail and covers less paper

Exactly — a small second number means less ground per centimetre, so more detail. Now for the conversion: measure the map distance in cm, multiply by the scale's second number to get ground centimetres, then divide by 100,000 to turn centimetres into kilometres.

Try it on this one.

On a map with a scale of 1:200,000, a measured distance of 3 cm represents how many kilometres on the ground?
A) 3 km
B) 6 km
C) 20 km
D) 60 km
b, 6 km

Exactly — 3 × 200,000 = 600,000 cm, and dividing by 100,000 gives you kilometres.

If a map shows a scale bar where 2 cm equals 5 km, what is the ground distance represented by 6 cm on the map?
A) 7.5 km
B) 15 km
C) 10 km
D) 20 km
a, 7.5 km

Not quite — check the direction of the scaling: 6 cm is bigger than 2 cm, so the ground distance must come out bigger than 5 km, not smaller. Ask yourself how many times 2 cm fits into 6 cm, then apply that same multiplier to the 5 km. Which option does that give you?
ohh wait, so 6 divided by 2 is 3, then 3 times 5 is 15, so b

Exactly — you found the multiplier and applied it to the ground distance, which is the whole trick with scale bars. That same idea matters when the route isn't straight: a string traces every bend, so the map length you measure is longer than a straight line, and the scale converts all of it.

Next: **Why is the straight-line distance between two cities often significantly shorter than the distance along the actual road network?**
A) Because straight lines distort on maps
B) Because roads curve around obstacles, terrain, and existing infrastructure
C) Because the map scale changes between measurements
D) Because cars travel faster on curved roads
c, because the map scale changes between measurements

Not quite — a map's scale is fixed for the whole sheet, so it stays the same no matter how many measurements you take. Think about a real journey instead: picture the road from your home to the nearest town, and ask why the tarmac can't just run dead straight between the two points. What physical things on the ground force the road to bend?

Welcome! Today you'll explore weathering — how the granite of our Seychelles islands gets broken down by physical, chemical, and biological processes.

Here's your warm-up: think about a rock that hasn't cracked or crumbled at all, but has clearly changed colour.

**Which of the following is a characteristic that distinguishes chemical weathering from physical weathering?**
A) Chemical weathering produces sand and gravel fragments of the original rock
B) Chemical weathering alters the chemical composition and mineral structure of the rock
C) Chemical weathering only occurs in tropical climates with high rainfall
D) Chemical weathering is faster than physical weathering in all environments
B

Exactly — chemical weathering changes what the rock is *made of*, not just its size, which is why a colour-changed boulder can still be perfectly solid. Now think about temperature instead of chemistry.

In Seychelles, freeze-thaw weathering is rare because the islands have a tropical climate with consistently warm temperatures. Which of the following best explains why freeze-thaw weathering is more common in mountain regions and high latitudes?
A) Mountains and high latitudes receive less rainfall than tropical islands
B) Temperatures regularly drop below freezing, allowing water in rock cracks to freeze and expand repeatedly
C) The rocks in mountains are softer and more easily broken by ice
D) Chemical weathering does not occur in cold climates, so physical weathering must occur instead
B

Exactly — repeated freezing expands the water by about 9% each time, prising the crack wider until the rock splits. That's physical weathering: the pieces are smaller but still the same mineral. Chemical weathering is different — it changes what the rock is actually made of.

Which of the following is the strongest evidence that a rock has undergone chemical weathering?
A) The rock is rounded and smooth in shape
B) The rock's mineral composition and chemical properties have been altered
C) The rock has broken into smaller fragments
D) The rock shows signs of being ground or scraped by water or ice
B

Exactly — a change in the minerals themselves is the fingerprint of chemistry at work, whereas breaking or smoothing leaves the rock chemically the same. Let's push that into a real Seychelles setting where several clues appear at once.

A rock face at the base of a Seychelles cliff shows deep cavities, small plant roots penetrating cracks, lichens covering portions of the surface, and some orange discoloration. If you were to identify the MOST DOMINANT weathering process affecting this rock face, what evidence would you prioritize?
A) The deep cavities, because they indicate the most physical damage
B) The orange discoloration, because it indicates chemical alteration of minerals
C) The plant roots and lichen presence, because biological agents must be dominant
D) The combination of cavities, discoloration, and organism presence; biological and chemical weathering together are most dominant
D

Exactly — real rock faces rarely show just one process, and reading all the evidence together is the right habit. Lichens are worth singling out, though, because they weather rock in a way roots do not.

Lichens contribute to biological weathering by producing which of the following?

A) Mechanical pressure through rapid growth that pushes rocks apart
B) Organic acids that dissolve minerals and weaken rock surfaces
C) Water that freezes and expands within rock cracks
D) Salt deposits that crystallize on rock surfaces and break them apart
B

Exactly — every ball is one possible outcome, so you add both colours together. Probability is then favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, so drawing a red ball would be 7 out of that total.

Which of the following best describes a V-shaped river channel?
A) Wide and shallow with gentle sloping banks

B

Where on a river channel cross-section diagram would you measure the width of the river?
A) From the riverbed to the water surface

D) Shallow braided channels with extensive deposition
B

Exactly — steep peaks mean fast water cutting downwards, so the channel stays narrow and deep relative to its width.

Now let's push that idea across a whole river system, comparing depth against width.

In comparing three river sections (A: steep mountain stream, B: transitional middle section, C: broad coastal plain), which sequence correctly orders them by typical depth-to-width ratio from highest to lowest?
A) A > B > C
B) C > B > A
C) B > A > C
D) A > C > B
A

Exactly — the narrow, deeply incised mountain stream is relatively deep for its width, while a coastal plain river spreads out wide and shallow.

Try this: **Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One corresponding angle measures 120°. What is the measure of the other corresponding angle?**

Exactly — corresponding angles sit in the same position at each intersection, so they're always equal when the lines are parallel.

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If one corresponding angle is 40°, what is the other corresponding angle?
A) 90°
B) 140°
C) 70°
D) 40°
d
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A corresponding angle to angle x is 135°. Find x.

Spot on — corresponding angles are equal, so x matches the given angle exactly, no subtraction needed.

Let's shift to a different angle pair now.

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 40°. What is the sum of both co-interior angles?

Spot on — co-interior angles sit on the same side of the transversal and always make a straight-line pair.

Now back to alternate interior angles, which are equal rather than supplementary.

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If one alternate interior angle is 125°, find the other alternate interior angle y.

Exactly — alternate interior angles are equal. The same pairing works OUTSIDE the two parallel lines: alternate **exterior** angles sit on opposite sides of the transversal but in the outer regions (above the top line and below the bottom line), and they are equal too.

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One alternate exterior angle measures 105°. What is the measure of the other alternate exterior angle?

Correct — nice work. Try this one:

Lines l and m are parallel, cut by transversal t. Angle 3 = 72°. Find angle 6 (the alternate interior angle).

Spot on — alternate interior angles are equal. Now the new pair: **co-interior** (same-side interior) angles sit on the SAME side of the transversal and both between the parallel lines, and they are the odd ones out — they are not equal, they are supplementary, adding to 180°.

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 60°. What is the measure of the other co-interior angle?

Exactly — co-interior angles sit on the same side of the transversal and always add to 180°, so 180 − 60 gives you that.

Yes — that mirror position makes them equal, so alternate exterior angles always match each other. The same mirror logic works *inside* the parallel lines too, and that pair has its own name.

B) 81°

Exactly. Now move outside the parallel lines: **alternate exterior angles** sit on opposite sides of the transversal but in the outer regions (above the top line and below the bottom line) — and like their interior cousins, they're equal when the lines are parallel.

The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.7. What is the probability that it does NOT rain?

Exactly — an event and its complement always fill up the whole probability scale, so they add to 1.

Here's one with a die instead of weather.

The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6. What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6?
A) 1
B) 0.2
C) 0.833333
D) 0.166667
C

Exactly — you subtracted 1/6 from 1 to get the "not a 6" outcome. That's the complement rule at work: P(event) + P(not event) = 1, so knowing one always gives you the other by subtraction.

The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.8. What is the probability that it does NOT rain?

Got it — that's right. Here's the next one:

A crab is caught with probability 0.7. Express as a decimal the probability the crab is NOT caught.

Exactly — 1 minus the probability of the event gives the probability it doesn't happen. Let's apply the same rule to a shop situation.

Spot on — 1 − 0.8 gives the complement. Here's one with a slightly different setup.

Exactly — 0.4 + 0.1 + 0.5 = 1, so the three outcomes cover everything. Whenever you find a "leftover" probability like this, add all your values back up to confirm they total 1.

Exactly — and 0.60 + 0.40 = 1, which is the check that confirms the two events are complements.

If P(sun) = 0.2, write the equation for P(no sun) and solve it.

Exactly — you wrote the equation out properly and solved it. The same subtraction works whenever you know one outcome and want its opposite.

Which of the following is the best definition of physical weathering?
A) The breakdown of rock by chemical reactions that change its mineral composition
B) The mechanical breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition
C) The weathering of rock caused exclusively by living organisms such as plants and lichens
D) The slow erosion of rock by water movement over thousands of years
B

Exactly — physical weathering breaks the rock apart mechanically, like when heating and cooling on a sun-baked Anse Royale boulder makes its outer layers peel off, but the mineral makeup stays the same. Chemical weathering is the opposite story: the rock's actual minerals get changed.

Which of the following is a characteristic that distinguishes chemical weathering from physical weathering?
A) Chemical weathering produces sand and gravel fragments of the original rock
B) Chemical weathering alters the chemical composition and mineral structure of the rock
C) Chemical weathering only occurs in tropical climates with high rainfall
D) Chemical weathering is faster than physical weathering in all environments
B

Exactly — physical weathering only makes smaller pieces of the same rock, while chemical weathering changes what the rock is actually made of. Now apply that to a trickier case where the rock hasn't broken at all.

You observe a boulder that is mechanically intact but shows significant color change, mineral transformation, and visible oxidation. A geologist argues this is predominantly physical weathering; another argues it is predominantly chemical weathering. Who is correct and why?
A) The first geologist is correct because the boulder is mechanically intact and unbroken
B) The second geologist is correct because color change, mineral transformation, and oxidation all indicate chemical alteration of the rock's composition
C) Both are partially correct because physical and chemical weathering always occur together
D) Neither can be correct without knowing the climate history of the boulder

B

the boulder hasn't broken apart but the minerals have changed, so that's chemical weathering. color change and oxidation mean the rock's composition changed, not just the size.

Exactly — staying whole while the minerals change is the signature of chemical alteration, since chemical weathering attacks composition rather than size. Now push that reasoning into a case where both processes have left their mark.

A piece of granite shows a combination of angular fragments (suggesting recent physical weathering) along with visible rust stains and areas where minerals appear altered. Which of the following sequences of weathering is most likely?
A) Chemical weathering occurred first, then physical weathering fragmented the weakened rock
B) Physical weathering broke the rock, then chemical weathering altered the exposed minerals
C) Physical and chemical weathering occurred simultaneously without any particular sequence
D) Biological weathering removed the outer layer, exposing fresh rock to physical weathering

B

physical weathering breaks it into pieces first, then chemical weathering gets to work on the fresh surfaces that are now exposed.

Exactly — fragmentation increases surface area, so chemical attack speeds up on the newly exposed faces. Now let's turn to living things: roots and burrows physically prise rock apart, while lichens release weak organic acids that eat into rock surfaces.

Which of the following is an example of biological weathering?
A) A granite boulder split by a freeze-thaw cycle in a mountain pass
B) A limestone cavern enlarged by carbonic acid in rainwater
C) A concrete pathway broken apart by growing tree roots and colonizing lichens
D) A pebble rounded by repeated tumbling in a river

C

tree roots physically break the concrete apart and lichens chemically alter it with acids.

C

Exactly — you multiplied the scale-bar value by the number of centimetres, which is the whole method.

A) 2 kilometres
B) 4 kilometres
C) 8 kilometres
D) 16 kilometres

ok so 1 cm is 2 km, and they're 8 cm apart so i times 2 by 8... thats 16

D

Exactly — multiply the map distance by what 1 cm stands for, and the units come out in km straight away. That same logic explains why the ratio number tells you how much ground each map covers.

How does decreasing the map scale (moving from 1:50,000 to 1:500,000) affect what can be shown on the map?
A) More area can be shown, but with less detail.
B) Less area can be shown, but with more detail.
C) More area can be shown, with the same amount of detail.

A

Exactly — you talked yourself right into it: bigger denominator means each centimetre swallows more ground, so more area fits on the sheet and detail has to be sacrificed.
